candidates.title: Why Did Rome's Richest Man Run a Fire Brigade That Let Your House Burn?
candidates.central_question: How did a city of wooden-floored tenements fight fires, and how did a private fire brigade turn a neighbour's disaster into profit?
candidates.angle: Start in a smoky stairwell with a bucket chain and a clerk haggling. Plutarch says Crassus bought burning buildings cheaply and then put out the fire. Then show Augustus's fix: the vigiles, a paramilitary fire watch with night patrols, hooks, buckets and fire-prevention rules.

Vigiles barracks (Excubitorium) in Trastevere
Insula remains at Ostia (Casa di Diana) and Herculaneum
Inscriptions naming the cohorts of vigiles
key_sources: Plutarch, Life of Crassus 2
Cassius Dio 55.26 (Augustus founds the vigiles)
Juvenal, Satires 3 (fire, collapse and noise in the insulae)
Digest 1.15 (duties of the praefectus vigilum)
risks: Plutarch's Crassus story is a hostile anecdote, so present it as reported by Plutarch rather than as audited fact
Do not overstate how effective the vigiles were; large fires such as 64 AD still happened

candidates.title: Why Was It Cheaper to Ship Grain Across the Sea Than to Haul It 300 Miles by Cart?
candidates.central_question: Why did Rome's overland transport cost so much that a cart of wheat could double in price on a long road?
candidates.angle: Break down the ox-cart: the load limit, the feed the oxen ate along the way, the axle grease and wear, tolls and breakdowns. Then compare it with a grain ship wallowing into Ostia. The empire's roads are famous, but its economy depended on water.

Roman wagon reconstructions and cart-part finds from Roman Britain and the Rhine frontier
key_sources: Diocletian's Price Edict (301 AD), transport rates
Cato, De Agri Cultura, on carts and draft animals
Columella, De Re Rustica
Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (transport cost analysis)
risks: The commonly quoted '300 miles doubles the price' is a modern calculation from late-antique rates, so state its dating clearly
Price Edict figures are maximum prices, not actual market prices

candidates.title: Were Roman Soldiers Really Paid in Salt?
candidates.central_question: Where does the 'salary comes from salt' story come from, and what did a legionary's pay actually look like after deductions?
candidates.angle: Debunk the popular myth with Pliny's etymology and then show the real mechanics: pay in coin, with stoppages for food, boots, hay and the unit's burial club. One surviving pay record shows how little cash a soldier actually held.
footage_evidence: archive probe "Roman legionary paymaster, wax tablet, army camp tent": 0 results
Papyrus pay and account records from Roman military units (Fink, Roman Military Records on Papyrus)
Roman legionary coin hoards and fort excavations
Tombstones of legionaries and standard-bearers
key_sources: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 31.89 (salt and salarium)
Fink, Roman Military Records on Papyrus (pay and stoppage accounts, including Papyrus Gen. Lat. 1)
Tacitus, Annals 1.17 (mutineer complaints about pay and deductions)
Speidel and Campbell on Roman army pay
risks: No ancient source confirms soldiers were paid in salt, so the video must present the myth as unproven rather than assert the opposite too strongly
Pay figures vary by era and unit, so pin them to a specific date such as the Domitianic rate

candidates.title: Why Did Romans Collect Pee on Street Corners?
candidates.central_question: How did the smell of Rome become a business, and who profited from it?
candidates.angle: Marble baths on one side and clay jars at street corners on the other. Follow a jar of urine from a Subura corner to the fuller's workshop, where it was used to clean wool and togas, and then to the emperor Vespasian, who taxed it.

key_sources: Suetonius, Vespasian 23 (the urine tax)

risks: The scale of the urine tax and the exact collection process are debated, so keep claims to what the sources support
Keep the tone observational rather than crude

candidates.title: How Did a Roman Fort at the Edge of the Empire Get Its Beer and Socks?
candidates.central_question: How did one frontier fort at Vindolanda get beer, grain, socks and spare sandals across muddy northern roads?
candidates.angle: Follow a single wooden tablet request, such as the beer complaint or the parcel of socks and underpants, back up the supply chain: the local brewer, the grain contractor, the ox-cart driver and the clerk who tracked it. Imperial roads meet the reality of mud, delays and a soldier asking for a clean pair of socks.

key_sources: Vindolanda Tablets, including the Masclus letter to Cerialis asking for beer

candidates.title: How Did Rome Hand Out Free Grain to 200,000 People With Clay Tokens and No Spreadsheets?
candidates.central_question: How did the annona dole identify, register and feed a city of citizens without databases?
candidates.angle: Walk through a recipient's month: the token (tessera), the queue, the granary clerk and the sack of wheat that still had to be milled and baked at home. Caesar had cut the rolls from 320,000 to 150,000 and Augustus capped them at around 200,000, so the question is who got in, who got cut and who profited from the paperwork.

key_sources: Suetonius, Divus Julius 41 (dole rolls cut from 320,000 to 150,000)
Cassius Dio 55.10 (Augustus and the number of recipients)

risks: Recipient counts differ between sources and periods, so scope the video to named reigns
Avoid claiming the dole fed the whole city; it did not, since many residents were not recipients
